questions.prompt: What do the SOLID principles aim to produce?

options.text: Mid-level software structures that are easy to understand, change comfortably, and are reusable
The fastest possible runtime performance
The smallest possible binary size
A single monolithic class

questions.explanation: SOLID aims to create mid-level structures (modules) that are easy to understand, allow comfortable changes, and are the basis of reusable components.

questions.prompt: Which rephrasing best captures the Single Responsibility Principle?

options.text: A module should be responsible to one, and only one, actor
A module should have only one method
A module should never be changed
A module should depend on every other module

questions.explanation: SRP: 'a module should have one, and only one, reason to change', rephrased as 'responsible to one, and only one, actor'.

questions.prompt: Which problems are symptoms of violating the SRP?

options.text: Accidental impact: a change for one actor breaks another
Merge collisions from different actors changing the same class
Shared algorithms affecting multiple actors
Faster compilation times

questions.explanation: SRP violation symptoms include accidental impact and merge collisions when code serving different actors is coupled (e.g. a shared ComputeAverage).

questions.prompt: The Open-Closed Principle states a software artifact should be...

options.text: Open for extension but closed for modification
Open for modification but closed for extension
Closed to all changes forever
Open to everyone on the team

questions.explanation: OCP (Bertrand Meyer): a software artifact should be open for extension but closed for modification — its behavior extendible without modifying the artifact.

questions.prompt: At the component level, the SRP corresponds to the Common Closure Principle and at the architectural level to the Axis of Change.
questions.explanation: SRP becomes the Common Closure Principle at the component level and the Axis of Change at the architectural level for creating architectural boundaries.

questions.prompt: How does OCP help the architect protect the system?

options.text: By arranging components in a dependency hierarchy that protects higher-level components from changes in lower-level ones
By forbidding all new features
By merging all components into one
By removing all interfaces

questions.explanation: Using OCP the architect divides the system into components arranged in a dependency hierarchy that protects higher-level components from changes in lower-level ones.

questions.prompt: The recommended action for SRP is to separate the code that different actors depend on.
questions.explanation: The action for SRP is to separate the code that different actors depend on, e.g. by separating data from functions or using the Façade pattern.
